# Palāyitajātaka (Ja 229)

**ID:** Ja 229
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Palāyitajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

According to its traditional frame narrative, the Buddha recounted this story while dwelling at Jetavana in connection with a mendicant with vagrant inclinations, beginning with the opening phrase, “Lo, my elephants”.

In studies of early Buddhist perspectives on conflict, the *Palāyitajātaka* is cited alongside Jātaka 181 and Jātaka 230 as a narrative illustrating the valorization of capturing an enemy alive (*jīvagrāham*) or prevailing over opponents through psychological intimidation rather than bloodshed [Jerryson and Juergensmeyer 2010].

**Sources**

- [Jerryson and Juergensmeyer 2010] Michael Jerryson and Mark Juergensmeyer, eds., Buddhist Warfare (2010) — Discussed the text's valorization of winning without bloodshed or taking enemies alive through intimidation.
